newsitem.title: UK: Currency set to rule Euro veg oils in week ahead.
newsitem.headline: Currency set to rule Euro veg oils in week ahead.

text.p: Currency factors look set to rule the European vegetable oil market during the coming week.
Traders said palm oil should head higher as producers increase prices up make for the weakness of the Malaysian ringgit and Indonesian rupiah against the U.S. dollar.
They added that the weaker Asian currencies could cause problems for the market in Asia unless prices rise.
"If they don't adjust their local prices to make up for the fall in currency players will export their oil rather than sell to the home market because they can get a better price." said one trader.
The fall in end-July Malaysian palm oil stocks gave sentiment a further boost and appeared to support feeling that exports are picking up.
However, European traders did not appear to be jumping on the bandwagon.
"There is no extra interest from Europe for palm oil, but coconut oil is a different story," said one trader.
Others said this was caused by the major differences between the Malaysian palm oil market and the Philippines coconut oil sector.
"In Malaysia the market is dominated by major plantations who, when they see the currency coming down, push up prices on the local market to make up for the losses," said one trader.
"However, in the Philippines the market is controlled by the little guy, who sees this as a chance to make some cash quickly," the trader added.
As a result more supplies of coconut oil will come on the market and European traders are expected to take advantage of this.
Prices have been falling steadily over the past few months and some traders feel that maybe it has gone far enough.
"We are in the mid five fifties and I think that is about as far as the market will going before it bounces back," said one trader.
Looking further ahead there could be problems from El Nino.
"If there is a long dry spell we could see problems in about nine months to a year, as the trees will be hit by drought stress," another trader said.
Another effect of El Nino could be a drop in power supplies to the crushers.
Most of the mills in the Philippines are driven by hydro electricity.
"If the water levels drop then they could have "brown outs" which means the wattage is cut back and the plants cannot run a full capacities," said a trader.
However, most traders agree that even if this does happen it is a long way off.
"The upside of this is an improvement in quality in the oil, because there will not be the rain around to stop the coconuts from drying out when they have been cut." said another.
In the soft oil sector traders will be eyeing the weather in the U.S. Midwest and currency.

"We saw some fund interest in soy oil Friday because they think that the monsoon will end early in India, but if this is the case the Indian could just as easily buy palm oil as soy oil" said one trader.
